q: According to 3.1, what is the real goal when evaluating a learning algorithm?
choices: Checking that the model performs well on new, unseen data
Driving the error on the training set as close to zero as possible
Making sure the model trains in the shortest possible time
Confirming that the model uses as few parameters as possible
why: Evaluation measures how well a model generalizes to unseen data. Low training error alone says nothing about that, and speed or parameter count are not the stated goal.

q: How does 3.1 define overfitting?
choices: Performing well on training data but poorly on test data
Performing poorly on both the training and the test data
Performing well on test data but poorly on training data
Performing equally well on both the training and test data
why: Overfitting = memorising the training set: great train score, bad test score. Poor on both is underfitting; good on both is what you want.

q: How does 3.1 define underfitting?
choices: Poor performance on both the training and the test data
Good performance on training data but poor on test data
Good performance on test data but poor on training data
Good performance on both the training and the test data
why: An underfit model is too simple to capture the pattern, so it does badly everywhere. Good-train/bad-test is overfitting.

q: A model scores 99% accuracy on the training set and 61% on the test set. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Overfitting: it memorised the training data and fails to generalize
Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the pattern
A well-fitted model, because the training accuracy is so high
Data leakage is certain, since test accuracy is above 50%
why: A big gap between high train and low test performance is the textbook sign of overfitting. Underfitting would be low on both.

q: A model scores 54% on the training set and 52% on the test set (two balanced classes). What is the diagnosis?
choices: Underfitting: it performs poorly on both sets
Overfitting: the train and test scores are too close
Good generalization, because the two scores are similar
Overfitting: the training score is above the test score
why: Similar scores are not automatically good: both are near chance level, so the model has not learned the pattern. That is underfitting.

q: Which of these is NOT one of the five reasons for evaluation listed in 3.1?
choices: Reducing the amount of memory the model needs
Model selection among several candidate models
Tuning hyperparameters for optimal performance
Benchmarking against baselines and earlier models
why: The five reasons are generalization ability, model selection, parameter tuning, understanding strengths and weaknesses, and benchmarking. Memory use is not on the list.

q: In 3.1, what does 'benchmarking' mean as a reason to evaluate?
choices: Comparing the model with baselines, earlier models or competitors' models
Measuring how long the model takes to train on a benchmark machine
Testing which hyperparameter setting gives the lowest training error
Checking whether the model is overfitting or underfitting the data
why: Benchmarking measures progress against baselines and other models. Hyperparameter search is 'parameter tuning' and the over/underfitting check is 'generalization ability'.

q: 3.1 says evaluation helps you understand a model's strengths and weaknesses. Which example does it give?
choices: A model may work well in high-dimensional spaces but poorly with noisy data
A model may train quickly on GPUs but slowly on ordinary CPUs
A model may need more memory on larger datasets than on small ones
A model may be easier to explain with fewer input features
why: The slide's example is a model that does well in high-dimensional spaces yet struggles with noisy data; evaluation reveals such behaviour.

q: Which set of metrics does 3.1 use for REGRESSION models?
choices: MSE, RMSE, MAE and R²
Accuracy, precision, recall and F1
Confusion matrix, accuracy and MSE
Precision, recall, R² and MAE
why: Regression predicts numbers, so it uses error-size metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE) and R². Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix are for classification.

q: Which pairing of task and metric is WRONG?
choices: Regression evaluated with precision
Regression evaluated with RMSE
Classification evaluated with F1-score
Classification evaluated with recall
why: Precision counts true and false positives, which only exist when predicting classes. RMSE is a regression metric; F1 and recall are classification metrics.

q: On the 3.1 slide 8 diagram, which algorithms appear under BOTH classification and regression?
choices: Decision tree and support vector machine
Naive Bayes and K-nearest neighbour
Logistic regression and linear regression
Ridge regression and stepwise regression
why: Decision tree and SVM are listed on both sides. Naive Bayes, KNN and logistic regression are under classification only; linear, ridge and stepwise regression under regression only.

q: Which formula is the MSE used in the course?
choices: 1 − Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − h(x⁽ⁱ⁾))² / Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − ȳ)²
why: MSE is the average squared error. The absolute-value version is MAE, the square-rooted one is RMSE and the 1 − ratio form is R².

q: Why does 3.1 call MSE 'sensitive to large errors'?
choices: Each error is squared, so big errors grow much faster than small ones
It divides by m, so a single large error dominates the average
It takes the square root, which magnifies the largest errors
It ignores the sign, so large negative errors are doubled
why: Squaring makes an error of 10 count 100 while an error of 1 counts 1. Dividing by m and ignoring sign do not single out large errors, and MSE has no square root.

q: What is the main reason to report RMSE instead of MSE?
choices: It gives the error in the same units as the target variable
It is much less sensitive to outliers than MSE is
It always produces a value between 0 and 1
It uses absolute values instead of squared errors
why: RMSE = √MSE, which undoes the squaring of units (e.g. dollars² → dollars). It is still outlier-sensitive and unbounded; absolute values are MAE.

q: According to 3.1, how does MAE compare with MSE?
choices: MAE is less sensitive to large errors than MSE
MAE is more sensitive to large errors than MSE
MAE and MSE always rank models the same way
MAE is the square root of the MSE value
why: MAE averages absolute errors, so a large error counts linearly rather than squared. The square root of MSE is RMSE, not MAE.

q: Predictions h = [2, 4, 6], true values y = [3, 4, 8]. What is the MAE?
why: Absolute errors are |2−3| = 1, |4−4| = 0, |6−8| = 2. Their mean is 3/3 = 1. 5/3 is the MSE; 3 is the sum, not the mean.

q: Predictions h = [2, 4, 6], true values y = [3, 4, 8]. What is the MSE?
why: Squared errors are 1, 0, 4; their sum is 5 and the mean is 5/3. 1 is the MAE, 5 forgets to divide by m, and 1.29 is the RMSE.

q: A model's MSE is 16. What is its RMSE?
why: RMSE = √MSE = √16 = 4.

q: Predictions h = [5, 7], true values y = [2, 10]. What are the MSE and MAE?
choices: MSE = 9, MAE = 3
MSE = 3, MAE = 9
MSE = 0, MAE = 3
MSE = 9, MAE = 0
why: The errors are +3 and −3. Squared: 9 and 9, mean 9. Absolute: 3 and 3, mean 3. A signed average would give 0, which is why the metrics square or take absolute values.

q: Absolute errors on four points are 1, 1, 1 and 9. Which statement is correct?
choices: MAE = 3 but MSE = 21: the one outlier inflates MSE far more
MAE = 3 and MSE = 3: both metrics treat the outlier equally
MAE = 21 but MSE = 3: the outlier inflates MAE far more
MAE = 12 and MSE = 84: neither metric divides by m
why: MAE = (1+1+1+9)/4 = 3. MSE = (1+1+1+81)/4 = 84/4 = 21. Squaring makes the single error of 9 dominate MSE.

q: In the course notebook, MSE = 11.7. Roughly what RMSE does it print?
choices: About 3.42
About 5.85
About 136.9
About 1.17
why: RMSE = √11.7 ≈ 3.42. 5.85 is MSE/2 and 136.9 is MSE², neither of which is RMSE.

q: What does R² represent?
choices: The proportion of variance in the target that the model explains
The average squared difference between predictions and targets
The fraction of all predictions that were exactly correct
The average absolute difference between predictions and targets
why: R² is the share of the target's variance explained by the model; close to 1 is a good fit. The average squared and absolute differences are MSE and MAE.

q: What is the CORRECT formula for R²? (ȳ is the mean of the true values.)
choices: 1 − Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − h(x⁽ⁱ⁾))² / Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − ȳ)²
1 − Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − h(x⁽ⁱ⁾))² / Σ(h(x⁽ⁱ⁾) − ȳ)²
Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − h(x⁽ⁱ⁾))² / Σ(y⁽ⁱ⁾ − ȳ)²
why: The denominator is the total sum of squares of the TRUE values around their mean. Slide 13 wrongly puts the predictions h(x) there; the notebook's ss_total = sum((y − y_mean)²) is correct.

q: 3.1 slide 13 prints R² with a mistake. What exactly is wrong?
choices: The denominator uses predictions minus the mean instead of true values minus the mean
The numerator uses absolute errors instead of squared errors between y and h(x)
The fraction is added to 1 instead of being subtracted from 1 in the formula
The mean ȳ is computed from the predictions instead of from the true values
why: The slide writes Σ(h(x) − ȳ)² in the denominator. It must be Σ(y − ȳ)², the variance of the true targets, as the notebook's ss_total does. Write the correct form in the exam.

q: What does R² = 0 tell you about a regression model?
choices: It does no better than always predicting the mean of y
It makes no errors at all on the evaluated data
It explains exactly half of the variance in y
It is always worse than predicting the mean of y
why: With R² = 0 the residual sum of squares equals the total sum of squares, i.e. the error of the 'predict ȳ' baseline. R² = 1 is perfect; R² < 0 means worse than the mean.

q: Can R² be negative?
choices: Yes, when the model is worse than simply predicting the mean
No, because it is a squared quantity it is always ≥ 0
No, it is always between 0 and 1 by definition
Yes, but only when the target values are negative
why: Despite the name, R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot. If SS_res > SS_tot the result is below 0, meaning the model loses to the constant-mean baseline. Negative targets have nothing to do with it.

q: SS_residual = Σ(y − h(x))² = 10 and SS_total = Σ(y − ȳ)² = 40. What is R²?
why: R² = 1 − 10/40 = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. 0.25 is the ratio alone; 4 and −3 come from flipping the ratio.

q: True values y = [1, 2, 3], predictions h = [1, 2, 4]. What is R²?
True values y = [2, 4, 6]. What is the total sum of squares Σ(y − ȳ)²?
why: ȳ = 4, deviations −2, 0, +2, squares 4, 0, 4, sum 8. This is the R² denominator.

q: Which statement about 'better' values is correct?
choices: Lower MSE/MAE is better, while higher R² (closer to 1) is better
Higher MSE/MAE is better, while lower R² (closer to 0) is better
Lower is better for all four: MSE, RMSE, MAE and R²
Higher is better for all four: MSE, RMSE, MAE and R²
why: MSE, RMSE and MAE measure error, so smaller is better. R² measures explained variance, so values near 1 are better.

q: In the notebook, which line computes the R² denominator correctly?
choices: ss_total = np.sum((y - y_mean)**2)
ss_total = np.sum((h_x - y_mean)**2)
ss_total = np.sum((y - h_x)**2)
ss_total = np.mean(np.abs(y - y_mean))
why: The total sum of squares uses the true y around its mean. (y − h_x)² is the residual sum (numerator); using h_x − y_mean repeats the slide-13 error.

q: What is a confusion matrix?
choices: A table of predicted versus actual classes: TP, FP, FN and TN counts
A table of feature correlations used to pick the input variables
A table of training versus test errors for each hyperparameter
A table of predicted probabilities for every example and class
why: It breaks predictions down against true labels into true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives.

q: What is a FALSE POSITIVE?
choices: The model predicted positive, but the actual class is negative
The model predicted negative, but the actual class is positive
The model predicted positive and the actual class is positive
The model predicted negative and the actual class is negative
why: 'Positive/negative' is what the model said; 'false' means it was wrong. So FP = said positive, really negative.

q: What is a FALSE NEGATIVE?
choices: The model predicted negative, but the actual class is positive
The model predicted positive, but the actual class is negative
The model predicted negative and the actual class is negative
The model predicted positive and the actual class is positive
why: FN = the model said negative and was wrong, so the case was really positive: a missed positive.

q: In the 3.1 fruit example, which class is positive?
choices: Banana is positive and apple is negative
Apple is positive and banana is negative
Whichever fruit the model predicts more often
Both fruits count as positive classes
why: The slide sets Banana = positive, Apple = negative before building the matrix.

q: Fruit example: TP = 4, FP = 2, FN = 1, TN = 3. What is the accuracy?
why: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total = (4 + 3) / 10 = 70%.

q: Fruit example: TP = 4, FP = 2, FN = 1, TN = 3. What is the precision?
why: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 4 / 6 ≈ 0.667. 4/5 is recall, 7/10 is accuracy.

q: Fruit example: TP = 4, FP = 2, FN = 1, TN = 3. What is the recall?
why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 4 / 5 = 0.8. 4/6 is precision.

q: Fruit example: precision ≈ 0.667 and recall = 0.8. What is the F1-score?
The slides put Predicted on the rows and Actual on the columns, but sklearn and the notebook print [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]. In the sklearn layout, what are the rows?
choices: The actual classes
The predicted classes
The feature values
The probability bins
why: sklearn's confusion_matrix has rows = actual and columns = predicted, the transpose of the slide-14 layout. Always check the axis labels before reading off TP/FP/FN/TN.

q: If you accidentally swap FP and FN when reading a confusion matrix, which metrics stay UNCHANGED?
choices: Accuracy and F1
Precision and recall
Precision and accuracy
Recall and F1
why: Accuracy uses only TP and TN, and F1 treats precision and recall symmetrically, so both survive the swap. Precision and recall trade places. Watch the axis labels in the fruit slides.

q: Which formula is accuracy?
choices: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
(TP + FN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
TP / (TP + FP)
TP / (TP + FN)
why: Accuracy = correct predictions / total predictions. TP/(TP+FP) is precision, TP/(TP+FN) is recall.

q: Which formula is precision?
choices: TP / (TP + FP)
TP / (TP + FN)
TN / (TN + FP)
(TP + TN) / total
why: Precision = true positives among everything predicted positive. TP/(TP+FN) is recall.

q: Which formula is recall?
choices: TP / (TP + FN)
TP / (TP + FP)
FN / (TP + FN)
(TP + TN) / total
why: Recall = true positives among all actual positives. TP/(TP+FP) is precision.

q: What other name does 3.1 give recall?
choices: Sensitivity
Specificity
Precision
Selectivity
why: The slide titles it 'Recall (Sensitivity)'.

q: How does 3.1 define the F1-score?
choices: The harmonic mean of precision and recall
The arithmetic mean of precision and recall
The geometric mean of accuracy and recall
The product of precision and recall
why: F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R), the harmonic mean. It balances the trade-off and gives one number that accounts for both.

q: Which question does precision answer?
choices: Of all the alarms the model raised, how many were real?
Of all the real positives, how many did the model catch?
Of all the predictions made, how many were correct?
Of all the real negatives, how many were labelled negative?
why: Precision looks only at predicted positives (the 'alarms'). Catching real positives is recall; all predictions correct is accuracy.

q: Which question does recall answer?
choices: Of all the real positives out there, how many did the model catch?
Of all the alarms the model raised, how many were actually real?
Of all the predictions made, how many of them were correct?
Of all the negatives predicted, how many were actually negative?
why: Recall looks only at actual positive cases and asks what fraction was found.

q: Precision 'ignores the negative predictions entirely'. Which confusion-matrix cells does it use?
choices: TP and FP only
TP and FN only
TP and TN only
FP and FN only
why: Precision = TP/(TP+FP): both cells are predicted-positive. Recall uses TP and FN (the actual positives).

q: Recall 'ignores how many false alarms were raised'. Which cells does it use?
choices: TP and FN only
TP and FP only
TN and FP only
TP and TN only
why: Recall = TP/(TP+FN), the actual-positive column. False alarms (FP) do not enter it at all.

q: For SPAM email detection, which metric does 3.1 say to prioritise?
choices: Precision, because a false positive buries a real email in spam
Recall, because every spam email must be caught at any cost
Accuracy, because spam and normal email are always balanced
Recall, because a false negative hides an important email
why: A false positive here means a job offer or client message lands in spam, which erodes trust. So precision is prioritised over catching every spam.

q: For CANCER screening, which metric does 3.1 say matters most?
choices: Recall, because missing a real cancer (FN) can be fatal
Precision, because a false alarm (FP) can be fatal
Accuracy, because both kinds of error cost the same
Precision, because doctors must avoid any extra tests
why: A missed cancer is far worse than a false alarm that only leads to another test, so doctors accept lower precision for higher recall.

q: For AIRPORT weapon detection, which metric matters most and why?
choices: Recall: missing a real threat is catastrophic, an extra bag check is minor
Precision: flagging an innocent bag is catastrophic, a missed threat is minor
Accuracy: almost every bag is harmless, so accuracy captures performance
Precision: security staff can only inspect a small number of bags per day
why: A false negative (missed weapon) is catastrophic; a false positive just means extra screening. That is the recall case.

q: General rule from 3.1: when a FALSE POSITIVE is expensive, embarrassing or harmful, prioritise...
choices: Precision
Recall
Accuracy
R²
why: Precision penalises false positives (FP is in its denominator). Recall is the choice when false negatives are costly.

q: General rule from 3.1: when a FALSE NEGATIVE is dangerous, costly or irreversible, prioritise...
choices: Recall
Precision
Accuracy
RMSE
why: Recall = TP/(TP+FN) drops whenever positives are missed, so it is the metric to protect when misses are costly.

q: 99% of transactions are legitimate. A model always predicts 'legitimate'. Which is true?
choices: Accuracy is 99% but recall for fraud is 0
Accuracy is 1% and recall for fraud is 0
Accuracy is 99% and recall for fraud is 99%
Accuracy is 50% because there are two classes
why: It is right on all 99% legitimate cases, so accuracy is 99%, yet it catches no fraud: recall = 0. That is why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

q: Why use F1 rather than just the average of precision and recall?
choices: The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller value, so one weak metric can't hide
The harmonic mean is pulled toward the larger value, rewarding one strong metric
The harmonic mean ignores recall and focuses on precision for imbalanced data
The harmonic mean always equals accuracy, so it is easier to interpret
why: With P = 1 and R = 0.1 the plain mean is 0.55 but F1 ≈ 0.18. F1 punishes being bad at either one.

q: A model flags very few cases as positive, and nearly all of those flags are correct, but it misses most real positives. What does it have?
choices: High precision, low recall
Low precision, high recall
High precision, high recall
Low precision, low recall
why: Few, correct alarms → FP small → high precision. Most positives missed → FN large → low recall.

q: A classifier labels EVERY example as positive. What is its recall?
choices: 1 (it catches every actual positive)
0 (it makes no negative predictions)
Equal to its accuracy on the data
Undefined, because FP is too large
why: With everything predicted positive, FN = 0, so recall = TP/(TP+0) = 1. Its precision, however, collapses to the share of positives in the data.

q: TP = 8, FP = 2, FN = 4, TN = 6. What is the precision?
why: Precision = 8/(8+2) = 0.8. 8/12 ≈ 0.667 is the recall; (8+6)/20 = 0.7 is the accuracy.

q: TP = 6, FP = 3, FN = 2, TN = 5. What is the recall?
why: Recall = 6/(6+2) = 0.75. 6/9 ≈ 0.667 is the precision and (6+5)/16 = 0.6875 is the accuracy.

q: TP = 40, TN = 50, FP = 5, FN = 5. What is the accuracy?
Precision = 0.5 and recall = 1.0. What is F1?
why: F1 = 2·0.5·1/(0.5+1) = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.667. The arithmetic mean would be 0.75; F1 sits closer to the smaller value.

q: Precision = 0.6 and recall = 0.6. What is F1?
why: When P = R, the harmonic mean equals that value: 2·0.36/1.2 = 0.6.

q: TP = 3, FP = 1, FN = 3, TN = 3. What is the F1-score?
TP = 5, FP = 0, FN = 5. What is the F1-score?
Predictions h = [1, 1, 0, 0], true labels y = [1, 0, 1, 0]. What is the precision?
Notebook classification example: TP = 2, FP = 1, FN = 2, TN = 5. What is the recall?
why: Recall = 2/(2+2) = 0.5. 0.667 is precision, 0.7 is accuracy and 0.571 is F1.

q: The notebook prints the confusion matrix [[5, 1], [2, 2]] built as [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]. Which entry is TP?
choices: The bottom-right 2
The top-left 5
The top-right 1
The bottom-left 2
why: The code builds np.array([[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]), so TP sits bottom-right. The top-left 5 is TN.

q: In the notebook, what happens to precision if the model predicts no positives at all (TP + FP = 0)?
choices: The code returns 0 instead of dividing by zero
The code raises a ZeroDivisionError and stops
The code returns 1, because no alarm was false
The code returns the accuracy value instead
why: Each metric is guarded with '... if denominator > 0 else 0', so an empty denominator gives 0.

q: Which is Bayes' theorem as written in 3.2?
choices: P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A) / P(B)
P(A|B) = P(A)·P(B) / P(B|A)
P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(B) / P(A)
P(A|B) = P(A|B)·P(A) / P(B)
why: Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.

q: In P(A|B) = P(B|A)·P(A)/P(B), what is P(A|B) called?
choices: The posterior
The prior
The likelihood
The evidence
why: P(A|B) is the updated probability of A after seeing B: the posterior. P(A) is the prior, P(B|A) the likelihood, P(B) the evidence.

q: In Bayes' theorem, what is P(A) called?
choices: The prior
The posterior
The likelihood
The evidence
why: P(A) is the belief about A before seeing B: the prior. In Naive Bayes it is the class frequency, e.g. P(Buy) = 10/15.

q: In Bayes' theorem, what is P(B|A) called?
choices: The likelihood
The prior
The posterior
The evidence
why: P(B|A), the probability of the observation given the class, is the likelihood. The likelihood tables in the shopping example hold exactly these values.

q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is P(two heads)?
why: The sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT}; only HH has two heads, so 1/4.

q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is P(at least one tail)?
why: HT, TH and TT contain a tail: 3 of 4 outcomes.

q: Two fair coins: what is P(second coin is heads | first coin is tails)?
why: Given the first is T, outcomes are TH and TT; one of two has a second head. Bayes gives (0.5·0.5)/0.5 = 0.5.

q: In the coin example, P(2nd = H | 1st = T) = P(2nd = H) = 0.5. What does this show?
choices: The two tosses are independent, so knowing the first changes nothing
Bayes' theorem gives wrong answers when probabilities are equal
The first coin toss always determines the second coin toss
The prior must always be 0.5 for Bayes' theorem to work
why: Conditioning on B left the probability of A unchanged, which is exactly what independence means.

q: Two fair coins: what is P(two heads | first coin is heads)?
why: Given the first is H, the outcomes are HH and HT; HH is one of two.

q: Where does the Naive Bayes classifier sit in the ML hierarchy on 3.2 slide 11?
choices: Supervised learning → classification
Supervised learning → regression
Unsupervised learning → clustering
Unsupervised learning → classification
why: It learns from labelled data and outputs a class, so supervised → classification.

q: On what principle does the Naive Bayes classifier work, according to 3.2?
choices: Conditional probability, as given by Bayes' theorem
Distances between points, as in nearest neighbours
Maximising the margin between two classes of data
Minimising squared error with gradient descent
why: Slide 4: the classifier works on the principle of conditional probability given by Bayes' theorem (Thomas Bayes, 1700s).

q: What is the 'naive' assumption in Naive Bayes?
choices: The features are independent of each other given the class
Every class has the same prior probability in the data
Every feature is normally distributed within each class
The features are irrelevant unless they are continuous
why: Assuming conditional independence lets the joint likelihood become a product: P(x₁,x₂,x₃|c) = P(x₁|c)·P(x₂|c)·P(x₃|c). Equal priors are not assumed.

q: In the 3.2 shopping example, what are the features and what is predicted?
choices: Features: day, discount, free delivery; predicted: whether the person buys
Features: price, discount, free delivery; predicted: the day of purchase
Features: day, price, product type; predicted: whether there is a discount
Features: buy, discount, day; predicted: whether delivery is free
why: The problem statement: predict whether a person will purchase given a combination of day (weekday/weekend/holiday), discount and free delivery.

q: The shopping dataset has 15 records, 10 Buy = Yes and 5 Buy = No. What is the prior P(Buy = Yes)?
why: The prior is the class frequency: 10 of 15 records bought.

q: How do you turn a frequency table into a likelihood table P(feature | class)?
choices: Divide each count by its class (column) total
Divide each count by the grand total of 15 records
Divide each count by its feature (row) total
Subtract each count from its class (column) total
why: P(Weekday | No) = 1/5 divides by the 5 No-records. Dividing by 15 gives a joint probability; dividing by the row total gives P(class | feature).

q: Day frequencies (Yes/No): Weekday 4/1, Weekend 2/2, Holiday 4/2. What is P(Weekday | Buy = No)?
why: Of the 5 No-records, 1 was a weekday. 4/10 is P(Weekday | Yes).

q: Discount frequencies: Yes → 8 buy / 2 no; No → 2 buy / 3 no. What is P(Discount = Yes | Buy = Yes)?
why: Divide by the 10 buyers: 8/10. 2/5 is P(Discount = Yes | No).

q: Free-delivery frequencies: Yes → 9 buy / 2 no; No → 1 buy / 3 no. What is P(Free delivery = Yes | Buy = No)?
why: Of the 5 No-records, 2 had free delivery. 2/11 would be P(No | FD = Yes), a different quantity.

q: There are 5 weekday, 4 weekend and 6 holiday records out of 15. What is P(Weekday)?
choices: 1/3 of the buyers
why: P(Weekday) is the evidence term: 5 weekday records out of 15.

q: Using P(Weekday | No) = 1/5, P(No) = 5/15 and P(Weekday) = 5/15, what is P(No Buy | Weekday)?
why: (1/5 · 5/15)/(5/15) = 1/5 = 0.20. Below 0.5, so a weekday customer most likely buys.

q: Using P(Weekday | Yes) = 4/10, P(Yes) = 10/15 and P(Weekday) = 5/15, what is P(Buy | Weekday)?
why: (4/10 · 10/15)/(5/15) = (4/15)/(5/15) = 4/5 = 0.8, the complement of the slide's 0.20. Directly: 4 of the 5 weekday records bought.

q: Slide 19 says 'out of the 30 people … 10 of those purchases were made on weekdays.' What do the tables actually show?
choices: 15 records, and 4 of the 10 purchases were on weekdays
30 records, and 10 of the 20 purchases were on weekdays
15 records, and 10 of the 15 purchases were on weekdays
30 records, and 4 of the 10 purchases were on weekdays
why: The dataset has 15 rows; weekday has 4 buys and 1 no-buy. 5/15 is simply P(Weekday). The slide's narrative is muddled but its 0.20 result is right.

q: Query: Holiday, Discount = Yes, Free delivery = Yes. What is the Naive Bayes numerator for Buy = No: P(D=Y|No)·P(FD=Y|No)·P(Hol|No)·P(No)?
why: All three No-likelihoods are 2/5, times the prior 1/3: 0.064/3 ≈ 0.0213. 0.192 is the Yes numerator and 0.1956 is the denominator.

q: Same query (Holiday, Discount = Yes, FD = Yes). What is the numerator for Buy = Yes?
why: 0.8 · 0.9 · 0.4 = 0.288, times the prior 2/3 gives 0.192. Forgetting the prior leaves 0.288.

q: Numerators: Yes ≈ 0.192, No ≈ 0.0213. After normalising, what is P(Buy) for this customer?
The slides get P(Buy|B) = 0.982 and P(No|B) = 0.109, which sum to 1.09. Why not 1?
choices: The shared denominator was itself computed assuming the features are independent
The likelihood tables contain an arithmetic mistake in the Holiday row
Naive Bayes probabilities never sum to 1 when there are three features
The priors 10/15 and 5/15 were accidentally swapped in the calculation
why: P(D=Y)·P(FD=Y)·P(Hol) = 0.1956 multiplies marginals as if independent, which is not the true P(B). Normalising (dividing by 1.09) fixes it.

q: Exam shortcut: why can you skip the denominator P(B) when classifying with Naive Bayes?
choices: It is the same for every class, so it doesn't change which class wins
It is always equal to 1 when the features are independent of each other
It is always smaller than the prior, so it can safely be ignored
It only matters for regression problems and not for classification
why: Every class's posterior is divided by the same P(B). Compare the numerators (0.192 vs 0.0213), then normalise if you need percentages.

q: Using the shopping tables, classify Weekend, Discount = No, Free delivery = No. (Yes: 2/10, 2/10, 1/10; No: 2/5, 3/5, 3/5.)
choices: No buy: 0.048 vs about 0.0027 for buy
Buy: about 0.0027 vs 0.048 for no buy
Buy: 0.048 vs about 0.0027 for no buy
A tie, because both scores equal 0.048

q: In 3.2's implementation, how does the naive_bayes() function compute a class score?
choices: Start with the prior, then multiply by the likelihood of each feature
Start with the evidence, then add the likelihood of each feature
Start with 1, then divide by the likelihood of each feature
Start with the prior, then add the log of each feature count
why: prob = prior(...); then for each feature, prob *= likelihood(...). The two class scores are then normalised to sum to 1.

q: What is the zero-frequency problem in Naive Bayes, and its fix named in 3.2?
choices: An unseen category gets probability 0 and zeroes the product; fix with Laplace smoothing
A feature with zero variance breaks the Gaussian formula; fix with feature scaling
A class with zero examples has an undefined prior; fix with oversampling the data
An empty test set gives zero accuracy; fix with a larger train/test split ratio
why: Because the likelihoods are multiplied, one zero wipes out the whole score. Laplace smoothing avoids zero counts.

q: Suppose no buyer ever shopped on a weekend, so P(Weekend | Yes) = 0/10. For a weekend query, what is the Buy = Yes score?
choices: 0, whatever the other likelihoods are
The product of the other two likelihoods
The prior P(Yes) = 10/15 on its own
Undefined, because you divide by zero
why: One zero factor makes the whole product zero. This is the zero-frequency problem that Laplace smoothing addresses.

q: Which is NOT an advantage of Naive Bayes listed in 3.2?
choices: Its independence assumption matches real-world data well
It doesn't require as much training data
It handles both continuous and discrete data
It is fast and usable for real-time predictions
why: The independence assumption is listed as a DISADVANTAGE: it rarely holds in real data. The others are on the advantages slide.

q: 3.2 says Naive Bayes has 'poor probability calibration'. What does that mean in practice?
choices: Use its outputs for ranking/classifying, not as true confidence scores
Its outputs are always exactly 0 or 1, so it cannot rank examples
It needs the probabilities to be calibrated before training starts
It can only be trained on features that have already been scaled
why: The output probabilities can be unreliable as confidences, but the ordering is usually good enough to pick a class.

q: On a heavily imbalanced dataset, how does Naive Bayes tend to behave?
choices: It skews toward the majority class
It skews toward the minority class
It ignores the class priors entirely
It becomes a lazy, distance-based learner
why: The prior P(class) multiplies every score, so a dominant class gets a head start. 3.2 lists this as 'imbalanced data bias'.

q: Which statement about Naive Bayes is an ADVANTAGE from 3.2?
choices: It is not sensitive to irrelevant features
It models interactions between features
It gives well-calibrated confidence scores
It never needs any smoothing of counts
why: Slide 27 lists 'not sensitive to irrelevant features'. It does NOT model feature interactions (independence assumption), is poorly calibrated, and may need Laplace smoothing.

q: Why is KNN called a NON-PARAMETRIC model?
choices: It learns no parameters; it simply memorises the training dataset
It has no hyperparameters at all, not even the number k
It assumes the data follows no distribution except a Gaussian
It learns weights but does not store the training data
why: KNN does not fit a discriminative function with learned weights; it stores the training set and compares new points to it. It still has hyperparameters (k, distance).

q: Why is KNN called a 'lazy' algorithm?
choices: There is no real training step; all the work happens at prediction time
It only looks at the single nearest neighbour to save computation
It stops training early once the error stops decreasing
It skips the features it considers irrelevant to save time
why: KNN just stores the data; distances are computed only when a new point must be predicted.

q: How does KNN produce a prediction for classification versus regression?
choices: Classification: majority vote of the k labels; regression: average of the k values
Classification: average of the k labels; regression: majority vote of the k values
Classification: label of the farthest point; regression: median of all points
Classification: weighted sum of all labels; regression: value of the nearest only
why: The slides: the most frequent value among the k neighbours for classification, the average of their values for regression.

q: KNN regression with k = 3: the three nearest neighbours have values 3, 5 and 7. What is predicted?
why: Regression KNN averages the neighbours: (3+5+7)/3 = 5.

q: KNN classification with k = 5: the five nearest labels are A, B, A, B, A. What is predicted?
choices: A
B
A tie
A or B at random
why: Majority vote: A has 3 votes, B has 2.

q: Which distance does 3.2 call the 'default' for KNN, suited to continuous features like height or salary?
choices: Euclidean
Manhattan
Hamming
Cosine
why: Euclidean is the shortest straight-line distance (Pythagorean theorem) and is the usual default for continuous features.

q: When does 3.2 recommend Manhattan distance?
choices: When movement is grid-like, e.g. features are whole integers
When features are continuous, like height, weight or salary
When the features are text and must be compared as strings
When there is only a single feature and no grid structure
why: Manhattan sums absolute coordinate differences, like walking city blocks; the slide suggests it for grid-distributed, integer-valued features.

q: In the Minkowski distance, which values of p give Manhattan and Euclidean?
choices: p = 1 → Manhattan, p = 2 → Euclidean
p = 2 → Manhattan, p = 1 → Euclidean
p = 0 → Manhattan, p = 1 → Euclidean
p = 1 → Euclidean, p = ∞ → Manhattan
why: Minkowski (Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|ᵖ)^(1/p): p = 1 is the sum of absolute differences, p = 2 is the square root of summed squares.

q: The Minkowski formula on 3.2 slide 37 is printed without an inner exponent. What is the correct form?
choices: (Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|ᵖ)^(1/p)
Σ(|xᵢ − yᵢ|^(1/p))ᵖ
(Σ(xᵢ − yᵢ))ᵖ
why: Each |xᵢ − yᵢ| must be raised to p before summing; otherwise p = 2 would not give Euclidean distance. The slide drops that ᵖ.

q: What is the Euclidean distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
why: √((4−1)² + (6−2)²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. 7 is the Manhattan distance; 25 forgets the square root.

q: What is the Manhattan distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
For the same two points, how do Manhattan and Euclidean distance compare?
choices: Manhattan is greater than or equal to Euclidean
Euclidean is always greater than Manhattan
They are always exactly equal to each other
It depends on whether k is odd or even
why: The straight line is the shortest path, so walking the grid (Manhattan) is never shorter. In the (1,2)–(4,6) example: 7 ≥ 5.

q: Iris example: new flower (5.2, 3.1), training flower (5.3, 3.7). What is their Euclidean distance?
why: √((5.2−5.3)² + (3.1−3.7)²) = √(0.01 + 0.36) = √0.37 ≈ 0.608. 0.70 is the Manhattan distance; 0.37 forgets the square root.

q: What are the three steps of KNN in the 3.2 iris example, in order?
choices: Find distances → rank them → take the k nearest and vote
Take the k nearest → find distances → rank them and vote
Rank the classes → find distances → average the features
Scale the data → train weights → apply a decision rule
why: Step 1 find distance, Step 2 find rank, Step 3 find nearest neighbours (then predict the majority).

q: Iris example, k = 3: the nearest neighbours are Setosa (0.22), Setosa (0.36), Setosa (0.608). What is the prediction for (5.2, 3.1)?
choices: Setosa
Versicolor
Virginica
No decision (tie)
why: All 3 votes are Setosa, so the new flower is classified as Setosa.

q: Iris example: rank 4 is Virginica (0.67) and rank 5 is Setosa (0.707). What would k = 5 predict?
choices: Setosa, with 4 votes against 1
Virginica, because it is ranked 4th
A tie between Setosa and Virginica
Versicolor, the most common in the data
why: The 5 nearest are Setosa, Setosa, Setosa, Virginica, Setosa: 4 to 1 for Setosa.

q: Query at (0, 0). Red points: (1, 0), (0, −1). Blue points: (0, 2), (2, 2), (3, 0). Euclidean KNN with k = 3 predicts...
choices: Red
Blue
A tie
Cannot tell
why: Distances: red 1, red 1, blue 2, blue ≈ 2.83, blue 3. The 3 nearest are red, red, blue → red.

q: Same data: query (0, 0); red at distances 1 and 1; blue at 2, ≈ 2.83 and 3. What does k = 5 predict?
choices: Blue
Red
A tie
Cannot tell
why: With k = 5 all points vote: 2 red vs 3 blue → blue. Changing k flipped the answer, as in the slide 47 picture.

q: In KNN, what happens at the extremes k = 1 and k = N (all points)?
choices: k = 1 uses only the closest point; k = N always predicts the majority class
k = 1 always predicts the majority class; k = N uses only the closest point
k = 1 and k = N both give the same predictions on any dataset
k = 1 averages all points; k = N uses only the farthest point
why: Slide 46: k can range from 1 (nearest neighbour only) to the dataset size (predicts the majority class of the whole dataset).

q: What is the effect of a very SMALL k in KNN?
choices: It tends to overfit: the boundary is noisy and follows individual points
It tends to underfit: the boundary becomes too smooth and simple
It makes KNN stop being lazy and start learning parameters
It has no effect; only the distance metric changes predictions
why: Low k reacts to every noisy point (overfitting). Higher k averages over a larger area and smooths the predictions.

q: What is the effect of a LARGER k in KNN, according to 3.2?
choices: It smooths the predictions by averaging over a greater area
It makes the model memorise individual noisy training points
It removes the need to store the training dataset in memory
It always lowers the error, so the largest k is the best
why: Higher k 'smooths' the prediction values; pushed too far it heads toward always predicting the majority class.

q: In the 3.2 slide 47 picture, what is the new point classified as with k = 3 and with k = 6?
choices: k = 3 → class B; k = 6 → class A
k = 3 → class A; k = 6 → class B
Class A for both values of k
Class B for both values of k
why: Inside the small circle B has the majority; the larger circle contains more A points, so the answer flips to A.

q: How does 3.2 recommend choosing the optimal k?
choices: Try several k on a train/test split and pick the elbow of the error curve
Always use k = 1, because the nearest point is the most informative
Set k equal to the number of features in the training dataset
Pick the largest k possible, because more votes means less error
why: Test different k, measure the error, and choose where increasing k gives only a tiny decrease while decreasing it sharply increases error: the elbow point.

q: Why does 3.2 split the data into training and test sets when choosing k?
choices: It allows an objective evaluation of each k on unseen data
It halves the memory KNN needs to store the training set
It lets KNN learn weights for each feature before predicting
It guarantees that the classes are perfectly balanced
why: Slide 48: separating training and test sets allows an objective model evaluation, linking back to 3.1's goal of measuring performance on unseen data.

q: In the 3.2 error-rate vs k plot, which k is chosen and why?
choices: k = 5, because the error rate becomes almost constant after it
k = 1, because the error rate is lowest at the very first point
k = 40, because the largest k always has the lowest error rate
k = 19, because the error rate peaks there before it drops
why: After k > 5 the error stabilises, so k = 5 is taken as the optimal (elbow) value.

q: For binary KNN classification, why is an odd k often recommended? (summary tip, not on the slides)
choices: So the vote between the two classes cannot end in a tie
So the distance computations run faster on odd numbers
So the model overfits less than with any even value of k
So the elbow point is guaranteed to fall on that value
why: With two classes, an odd number of voters always yields a strict majority. It is a practical tip, not a rule from the deck.

q: What does 3.2 mean by calling KNN 'adaptable'?
choices: As soon as new training samples are added, predictions take them into account
It automatically chooses the best distance metric for any kind of dataset
It adapts the value of k during training to minimise the training error
It can switch between classification and regression without any changes
why: Since KNN just stores the data, adding samples immediately changes future predictions without retraining.

q: Which hyperparameters does KNN need, according to 3.2?
choices: Just k and a distance metric
A learning rate and number of epochs
The prior and the likelihood tables
A kernel and a regularisation constant C
why: 'Easily programmable: kNN requires only a few hyper-parameters — a k value and a distance metric.'

q: Why is KNN 'difficult to scale'?
choices: It stores all the data and computes distances to every point at prediction time
It must retrain all of its weights from scratch whenever new data arrives
It can only handle two features, so larger datasets cannot be used
It needs an exponential number of epochs as the dataset grows
why: KNN takes a lot of memory and storage, and each prediction is computationally intensive because it compares against everything.

q: What is the 'curse of dimensionality' for KNN?
choices: With many dimensions, distances become less meaningful and accuracy drops
With many training points, the elbow method can no longer find a good k
With many classes, the majority vote always ends in a tie between them
With many neighbours, the algorithm forgets the closest training points
why: A fixed training set cannot keep up as dimensions grow: even 'similar' points end up far apart on other dimensions, so predictions get worse.

q: Feature 1 is salary (tens of thousands), feature 2 is age (tens). What goes wrong with unscaled KNN? (summary note, not on slides)
choices: Salary dominates every distance, so age barely affects the neighbours
Age dominates every distance, so salary barely affects the neighbours
Nothing, because Euclidean distance is unaffected by feature units
KNN refuses to run until the features have identical ranges
why: Distances add raw differences, so the large-unit feature swamps the small one. Scale features before KNN.

q: In the 3.2 KNN class, what does fit(X_train, y_train) do?
choices: It just stores X_train and y_train; no computation happens
It computes the distances between all pairs of training points
It learns one weight per feature using gradient descent
It sorts the training data by distance from the origin
why: fit only assigns self.X_train and self.y_train, the 'lazy' behaviour. Distances are computed in _predict.

q: In the 3.2 KNN code, how is the predicted label chosen in _predict?
choices: np.argsort(distances)[:k], then the most common label via np.bincount(...).argmax()
np.argmax(distances)[:k], then the mean of those labels via np.mean(...)
np.sort(labels)[:k], then the median label via np.median(...)
np.argmin(distances), then that single label is returned
why: argsort gives the indices of the k smallest distances; bincount + argmax returns the majority label.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts the two 3.2 classifiers?
choices: Naive Bayes is built from class-conditional probabilities; KNN from distances to stored points
Naive Bayes stores every training point; KNN builds frequency and likelihood tables
Both are unsupervised methods that need no labels to make their predictions
Both assume the features are independent of each other given the class
why: NB estimates priors and likelihoods and applies Bayes' theorem; KNN memorises the data and votes among the nearest points. Both are supervised; only NB makes the independence assumption.
